title: Human Heart Anatomy: Chambers, Valves & Coronary Vessel
description: Master human heart anatomy with our illustrated guide to all four chambers, four valves, coronary blood vessels, myocardial layers, and electrical impulse.
h1: Human Heart Anatomy: Chambers, Valves, Vessels and Conduction
blurb: Two synchronized muscular pumps in one organ: four chambers, four one-way valves, coronary arteries, and the intrinsic SA-to-Purkinje electrical pacemaker.
lead: Roughly the size of a closed fist and beating about 100,000 times every day, the human heart is two synchronized muscular pumps sealed inside a single organ. In this illustrated guide to human heart anatomy, we examine 22 documented structures—including superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, aorta, pulmonary trunk—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Roughly the size of a closed fist and beating about 100,000 times every day, the human heart is two synchronized muscular pumps sealed inside a single organ. The heart is a double pump. Its right side receives deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae and sends it to the lungs; its left side receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins and ejects it into the aorta. The two sides never mix because of the interatrial and interventricular septa, and one-way valves keep blood moving forwards. Contraction is triggered by an electrical impulse that begins in the sinoatrial node and sweeps through the atria, the atrioventricular node, the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibres. Within the human body, the heart (Cor) is situated in middle mediastinum, behind the sternum, receives arterial perfusion via right & left coronary arteries (first branches of the aorta), and is innervated by cardiac plexus — vagus (slows) + sympathetic T1–T4 (speeds up).

The superior vena cava (Vena cava superior) is the large vein draining the head, neck, upper limbs and thorax. It enters the upper part of the right atrium. Physiologically, the superior vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from everything above the diaphragm. The inferior vena cava (Vena cava inferior) is the largest vein in the body. It collects blood from the abdomen, pelvis and lower limbs and enters the inferior part of the right atrium. Physiologically, the inferior vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from below the diaphragm. The aorta is the largest artery in the body. It arises from the left ventricle, arches over the left main bronchus and descends through the thorax and abdomen. Physiologically, the aorta distributes oxygenated blood to the entire systemic circulation. The pulmonary trunk (Truncus pulmonalis) leaves the right ventricle and divides into right and left pulmonary arteries. Uniquely, it carries deoxygenated blood. Physiologically, the pulmonary trunk carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for oxygenation. The pulmonary veins (Venae pulmonales) are four veins — two from each lung — that carry freshly oxygenated blood into the left atrium. Physiologically, the pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart. The myocardium is the thick middle layer of the heart wall, made of branching, interlinked cardiac muscle fibres joined by intercalated discs. Physiologically, the myocardium contracts to generate the pressure that ejects blood.

Clinically, regarding the superior vena cava, obstruction (SVC syndrome) causes facial and arm swelling with distended neck veins. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the inferior vena cava, compression in late pregnancy reduces venous return and can cause supine hypotension. In clinical pathology involving the aorta, a tear in the wall (aortic dissection) causes sudden tearing chest or back pain — a surgical emergency. Medical evaluation of the pulmonary trunk also notes that a clot lodging here (pulmonary embolism) causes breathlessness, pleuritic pain and hypoxia.

questions.question: How many chambers does the heart have?
questions.answer: The heart has two upper receiving chambers, the right and left atria, and two lower pumping chambers, the right and left ventricles. The right ventricle sends blood to the lungs; the left sends it to the body.

questions.question: What route does blood take through the heart?
questions.answer: Body blood enters the right atrium, passes through the right ventricle to the lungs, returns to the left atrium, then moves through the left ventricle into the aorta.

questions.question: Why is the left ventricular wall thicker?
questions.answer: The left ventricle must generate greater pressure to move blood through the systemic circulation. Its myocardium is therefore thicker than that of the right ventricle, which pumps into the lower-pressure pulmonary circulation.

questions.question: Do coronary arteries carry blood through the heart chambers?
questions.answer: No. Coronary arteries branch near the aortic root and supply the heart muscle itself. The blood passing through the chambers does not directly nourish the full thickness of the myocardium.

questions.question: How do heart valves keep blood moving forward?
questions.answer: Tricuspid and mitral valves guard the atrioventricular openings; pulmonary and aortic valves guard ventricular outflow. They open and close in response to pressure changes, limiting backward flow rather than actively pumping blood.
